figures.caption: Fig. 6. Synergistic evolution of force chain density, strength, and orientation of coated particles during calendering. (a-d) depict the contact force network of the particles at compression rates of 10 %, 20 %, 30 %, and 40 %, respectively. The force chain network becomes denser and more stable as the compression rate increases. (e-h) show the three-dimensional distribution of the contact fabric, the radial length represents the orientation strength in that direction, and the colorbar represents the contact strength in that direction. (i) represents the probabilistic distribution of the contact strength at different compression rates, and the strong and weak force chains are distinguished at the point of f = 1. (j) displays the diagonal component of the contact deviation tensor, describing the change in contact anisotropy under compression. (k) exhibits the proportion of strong force chains, which can be obtained from the contact force probability distribution curve. (l) captures the number of particle contact pairs at different compression levels, which indirectly reflects the force chain density. (m) demonstrates the diagonal components of the coating mechanical stress and total stress tensor at different compression ratios. The overall strength of the coating stresses represents the mechanical response of the system to the action of the strong force chain.

figures.caption: Fig. 10. Contact damage on collector surfaces is affected by particle diameter. (a-c) show the DEM models for particle diameters of 7 μm, 9 μm and 13 μm, respectively, corresponding to the D50 values of the particle size distributions. The increase in particle size leads to changes in the particle contact network. (d-f) depict the corresponding force chain structure at 40 % compression rate. As the particle diameter increases, the force chains become more continuous and concentrated. (g-i) display the stress distribution on the surface of the current collector, the more localized stress concentration points are generated as the particle diameter increases. (j-l) show the magnified morphology on the aluminum foil surface after calendering, and the results show that as the particle size increases, the damage area also increases. (m-n) demonstrate the comparison of simulated and experimental values of embedding diameter and depth to verify the model's accuracy. (o) depicts the embedding behavior curves for different particle sizes at a 40 % compression rate, which reveals the competitive relationship between damage points and stress values. (p) demonstrates the relationship between compression rate, particle diameter, and stress on the collector.

figures.caption: Fig. 11. Effect of particle distribution on collector surface damage. (a-c) show the coated particles in the DEM model under different particle distribution conditions (σ = 0.5, σ = 2 and σ = 4). (d-f) display the corresponding normal overlap between the AM particle layer and the current collector, highlighting that the increase in particle dispersion causes more embedded regions. (g) depicts the distribution of pits on the surface of the current collector at a compression rate of 40 % for the three distribution conditions. Higher dispersion (σ = 4) results in deeper and more widely distributed pits. (h) shows the comparison of maximum collector stress for different particle size and dispersion configurations. (i) exhibits a three-dimensional surface plot of the relationship between compression rate, PSD, and collector stress, which suggests that an increase in compression rate and particle dispersion together intensifies the mechanical loading on the collector, thereby accelerating structural damage.
